questions.q: What is the Pauli-operator form of the Max-Cut cost Hamiltonian for an edge (i,j)?
options: X_i X_j
½(I - Z_i Z_j)
Z_i + Z_j
½(X_i + X_j)
questions.explain: The cost Hamiltonian per edge is ½(I - Z_i Z_j), since Z_i and Z_j have eigenvalues ±1 matching the Ising spins s_i = 1-2x_i, and this expression equals 1 when the edge is cut and 0 otherwise.

questions.q: What is the standard mixer Hamiltonian H_B used in QAOA, and why is Pauli-X chosen rather than Pauli-Z?
options: H_B = Sum of X_i; X is chosen because it does not commute with Z and physically flips qubits, which is what redistributes measurement probability
H_B = Sum of Z_i; Z is chosen because it matches the cost Hamiltonian exactly
H_B = Sum of Z_i Z_j interaction terms, just like the cost Hamiltonian
H_B has no standard form and differs randomly on every QAOA run
questions.explain: H_B = Sum_i X_i is the standard choice because X doesn't commute with Z -- it flips qubits between |0> and |1>, which is the only way to actually move probability mass between basis states, since Z-based phases alone never change measurement probabilities.

questions.q: Why is it essential, not a flaw, that H_C and H_B do not commute?
options: Because if they commuted, alternating them would be pointless -- applying them in either order or merging them would give the same result, so non-commutation is exactly what makes repeated alternating layers meaningful
Because commuting operators are always physically impossible to implement on real hardware
Because non-commuting operators always produce a perfect solution to any QUBO
Because QAOA requires H_C and H_B to have the same eigenvalues
questions.explain: If [H_C, H_B] = 0, the cost and mixer unitaries could be merged into a single operator with no benefit from alternating -- the non-commutation (stemming from [Z,X] != 0) is precisely what lets repeated layers sculpt the probability distribution more precisely.

questions.q: Why does the mixer unitary e^(-i*beta*H_B) factor into independent single-qubit rotations, one per qubit?
options: Because H_B = Sum_i X_i has no cross-qubit interaction terms, so its exponential splits into a tensor product of single-qubit X-rotations
Because the cost Hamiltonian forces the mixer to act on all qubits simultaneously as one block
Because quantum computers cannot implement multi-qubit gates
Because beta is always equal to zero in practice
questions.explain: Since H_B sums independent single-qubit X_i terms with no coupling between qubits, the exponential e^(-i*beta*H_B) factors cleanly into a separate rotation on each qubit -- which is exactly the per-qubit 2x2 matrix form used in the Lesson 6 simulation.

questions.q: In the exact single-edge simulation from Lesson 6, what per-basis-state cost values does H_C = ½(I - Z_0 Z_1) assign to |00>, |01>, |10>, and |11>?
options: 0, 1, 1, 0 respectively
1, 0, 0, 1 respectively
0, 0, 1, 1 respectively
1, 1, 1, 1 respectively
questions.explain: Z_0Z_1 has eigenvalue +1 on |00> and |11> (same spin) and -1 on |01> and |10> (opposite spins), so ½(1-(+1))=0 for |00>/|11> and ½(1-(-1))=1 for |01>/|10> -- exactly matching the cut-indicator values used in the simulation.
